questions.question: Let $X_1,\dots,X_n$ be iid with density $f$ and CDF $F$, where $n\ge2$. Which formula gives the density of $X_{(k)}$ for every integer $1\le k\le n$?

Let $X_1,\dots,X_n$ be iid continuous observations with density $f$ and CDF $F$, and let $2\le k\le n$. In the density $nf(x)\binom{n-1}{k-1}F(x)^{k-1}(1-F(x))^{n-k}$ of $X_{(k)}$, what does $F(x)^{k-1}$ represent?
options: The probability that a specified group of $k-1$ observations all fall below $x$
The probability that a specified group of $k-1$ observations all fall above $x$
The probability that all $n$ observations fall below $x$
The number of choices of $k-1$ observations from the other $n-1$

questions.question: Let $X_1,\dots,X_n$ be iid with common CDF $F$, and let $M=\max_iX_i$. Why is $\mathbb{P}(M\le x)=F(x)^n$?
options: Identical distributions make the observations share one realised value.
The event $M\le x$ requires at least one observation to be at most $x$.
The events $X_i\le x$ are disjoint, so their probabilities multiply.
The event $M\le x$ requires all observations to be at most $x$.

questions.question: Which expression is the CDF of the minimum $X_{(1)}$ of iid $X_1,\dots,X_n$ with CDF $F$?
Let $X_1,\dots,X_n$ be independent continuous observations with possibly different CDFs $F_1,\dots,F_n$, where $n\ge2$. Which formula always gives the CDF of $M=\max_iX_i$?
For the maximum of four iid $\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)$ variables, what is the value of the density at $x=\tfrac12$?
Three iid $\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)$ numbers are drawn. How likely is it that the smallest is at most $\tfrac12$?
Which density does the median $X_{(2)}$ of three iid $\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)$ variables have on $(0,1)$?
The maximum of three iid $\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)$ variables has density $3x^2$ on $(0,1)$. What is its mean?
Two components have iid $\operatorname{Exp}(1)$ lifetimes. What is the probability that the longer lifetime exceeds $1$?
Let $X_1,\dots,X_n$ be iid with CDF $F$, where $n\ge2$. Which formula gives $\mathbb{P}(X_{(k)}\le x)$ for every real $x$ and every integer $1\le k\le n$?
For $n\ge5$ iid continuous observations, the density of $X_{(3)}$ has counting coefficient $n\binom{n-1}{2}=n!/[2!(n-3)!]$. Why are the factorials $2!$ and $(n-3)!$ in the denominator?
options: They remove permutations within the groups below and above the third-ranked observation.
They remove choices of the observation occupying third rank from the count.
They correct for ties among observations below and above the third rank.
They convert an unordered choice of three observations into a fully ordered sample.

questions.question: Let $X_1,\dots,X_n$ be iid continuous observations with CDF $F$, where $n\ge2$. Choose $t$ with $0<F(t)<1$, and define $A=\{X_{(1)}>t\}$ and $B=\{X_{(n)}\le t\}$. Are the minimum and maximum independent?
options: Yes, because independence of the observations makes $A$ and $B$ independent.
No, because $A$ and $B$ are disjoint but each has positive probability.
Yes, because the minimum and maximum occupy different sample ranks.
No, because continuous observations give $A$ and $B$ zero probability.

questions.question: For three iid $\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)$ variables, what is $\mathbb{P}(X_{(2)}\le\tfrac14)$, the chance that the median is at most $\tfrac14$?
Four components have iid $\operatorname{Exp}(1)$ lifetimes. Which density does the time of the second failure, $X_{(2)}$, have for $x>0$?
Let $X_1,X_2,X_3$ be iid $\operatorname{Unif}(0,4)$ observations and $M=\max(X_1,X_2,X_3)$. What is $\mathbb{P}(1<M\le3)$?
Let $X_1,\dots,X_n$ be iid with common density $f$ and CDF $F$, where $n\ge3$. Which identity holds for every such distribution?

Let $X_1,\dots,X_n$ be iid discrete observations, where $n\ge2$, and let $M=\max_iX_i$. At a support point $a$, write $p=\mathbb{P}(X_i\le a)$ and $q=\mathbb{P}(X_i<a)$. Which expression always gives $\mathbb{P}(M=a)$?
Four iid $\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)$ observations have minimum $L$ and maximum $M$. What is $\mathbb{P}(L\le\tfrac13,\ M>\tfrac23)$?
How many iid $\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)$ numbers are needed, at the least, for the largest to exceed $0.9$ with probability at least $\tfrac12$?
